group.title: Law
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The person who brings a case against someone in a court.
examples: The {plaintiff} said the company had broken its promise.
wrong: The plaintiff is the judge who decides the case.

words.meaning: The person who is accused or sued in a court.
examples: The {defendant} denied the charge.
wrong: The defendant is the lawyer who works for the court.

words.meaning: The decision of a jury or judge at the end of a trial.
examples: The jury returned a {verdict} of not guilty.
wrong: A verdict is the first question a lawyer asks a witness.

words.meaning: A formal statement that a witness makes in court.
examples: Her {testimony} helped the jury understand the events.
wrong: Testimony is the punishment that a judge gives to a criminal.

words.meaning: Legally responsible for something.
examples: The company is {liable} for the damage.
wrong: A person who is liable has no legal duty at all.

words.meaning: A case that a person or company brings to a court.
examples: She filed a {lawsuit} against her former employer.
wrong: A lawsuit is a suit that a lawyer wears in court.

words.meaning: An agreement that ends a legal dispute without a full trial.
examples: The two sides reached a {settlement} before the trial.
wrong: A settlement is the final decision of a jury after a long trial.

words.meaning: The official power of a court to make decisions about a certain area or subject.
examples: The case falls under the court’s {jurisdiction}.
wrong: Jurisdiction is the amount of money a person pays in a fine.

words.meaning: A failure to keep a law, a rule or the terms of an agreement.
examples: Missing the payment was a {breach} of the contract.
wrong: A breach is a promise that has been kept in full.

words.meaning: A separate part of a contract or law.
examples: The {clause} says that either side may cancel.
wrong: A clause is the person who signs a contract first.

words.meaning: To change the words of a law or document in order to improve it.
examples: Parliament voted to {amend} the law.
wrong: To amend a law is to keep it exactly as it was written.

words.meaning: To ask a higher court to change a decision.
examples: The company decided to {appeal} the ruling.
wrong: To appeal is to accept the decision and go home.

words.meaning: Money paid to a court so that an accused person can wait for trial outside prison.
examples: The judge set {bail} at five thousand dollars.
wrong: Bail is the money that a court gives to a witness.

words.meaning: A legal order that tells a person to come to court or hand over documents.
examples: The lawyer received a {subpoena} to produce the emails.
wrong: A subpoena is a prize that a court gives to a lawyer.

words.meaning: A failure to take proper care, which causes harm to another person.
examples: The hospital was sued for {negligence}.
wrong: Negligence is extreme care that prevents all harm.

words.meaning: A written law passed by a parliament or similar body.
examples: The {statute} bans smoking in public buildings.
wrong: A statute is a decision that a judge makes while a trial is running.

words.meaning: A person who sees an event and may tell a court what happened.
examples: The {witness} saw the accident from her window.
wrong: A witness is the person who is accused of the crime.

words.meaning: A claim that someone has done something wrong, made without proof yet.
examples: The company denied the {allegation} of fraud.
wrong: An allegation is a fact that has already been proved in court.

words.meaning: To decide in a court that a person is not guilty.
examples: The jury voted to {acquit} the defendant.
wrong: To acquit a person is to find that the person is guilty.

words.meaning: To decide in a court that a person is guilty of a crime.
examples: The jury did not {convict} him because the evidence was weak.
wrong: To convict a person is to declare that the person is innocent.

words.meaning: To bring a legal case against a person or company.
examples: They plan to {sue} the builder for the damage.
wrong: To sue someone is to give them a legal reward.

words.meaning: The legal right to control the copying and use of a creative work.
examples: The author owns the {copyright} to the book.
wrong: Copyright is the right of anyone to copy a book for free.

words.meaning: A name or symbol that legally belongs to one company’s product.
examples: The logo is a registered {trademark}.
wrong: A trademark is a mark made by a shoe on the floor.

words.meaning: A person who pays rent to use a house, an apartment or an office.
examples: The {tenant} paid the rent on the first of the month.
wrong: A tenant is the person who owns the building and receives rent.

words.meaning: A legal agreement to rent a property for a set period.
examples: We signed a one-year {lease} on the apartment.
wrong: A lease is the right to own a property forever without paying.

words.meaning: A person with legal authority to witness and confirm signatures on documents.
examples: The {notary} stamped the signed document.
wrong: A notary is the judge who runs a criminal trial.

words.meaning: A group of ordinary people who decide the facts in a trial.
examples: The {jury} listened to the evidence for three days.
wrong: A jury is a single judge who decides every case alone.

words.meaning: A lawyer, especially in the United States.
examples: Her {attorney} advised her not to speak to the press.
wrong: An attorney is a person who decides whether an accused person is guilty.

words.meaning: An official rule made by an authority.
examples: A new {regulation} bans plastic bags.
wrong: A regulation is a choice that nobody has to follow.

words.meaning: To bring a legal case against a person who is accused of a crime.
examples: The state will {prosecute} the thief.
wrong: To prosecute a person is to defend the person in court.
